title: Telco Customer Churn Analysis
text:
Customer churn — when customers stop doing business with a company — is one of the most expensive problems in the telecom industry. Acquiring a new customer typically costs five to seven times more than retaining an existing one, so understanding who churns and why is critical for any subscription-based business.
This project explores a public Telco customer dataset of roughly 7,000 subscribers, each described by demographic attributes (gender, senior citizen status, partner/dependents), account information (tenure, contract type, payment method, monthly charges), and the services they subscribe to (phone, internet, streaming, tech support, etc.). The goal is to identify the strongest churn drivers and translate them into actionable retention strategies.

Dashboard Overview
The dashboard is organized as a four-part story. Use the tabs at the top to move between sections:

Demographics — How churn rates differ across gender, age group, and family status.
Contract & Billing — The relationship between contract length, payment method, monthly charges, and churn.
Service Usage — Which add-on services (online security, tech support, streaming) correlate with retention.
Key Predictors — A summary of the strongest churn drivers and what they imply for retention strategy.

title: Telco Customer Churn Analysis
text:
Key Findings
Several patterns emerge consistently across the four stories:

Contract length is the single strongest predictor of churn. Customers on month-to-month contracts churn at a dramatically higher rate than those on one- or two-year contracts. Locking customers into longer agreements — through discounts or bundled perks — is likely the highest-leverage retention move.
Tenure matters more than demographics. New customers (under 12 months of tenure) are far more likely to leave than long-tenured ones, regardless of age or gender. The first year is the critical retention window.
Fiber optic internet customers churn more than expected, despite paying premium prices. This suggests a service-quality or price-perception issue worth investigating further.
Add-on services reduce churn. Customers with online security, tech support, or device protection are noticeably stickier — these services likely increase switching costs and perceived value.
Payment method correlates with churn, with electronic check users churning at the highest rate. This may reflect a less-engaged customer segment rather than a causal effect of the payment method itself.

title: Telco Customer Churn Analysis
text:
Recommendations
Based on the patterns above, three retention levers stand out:

Migrate month-to-month customers to longer contracts through targeted offers, especially in the first 6–12 months of tenure.
Audit the fiber optic experience — both technical reliability and pricing — to understand why these high-value customers are leaving.
Bundle add-on services (security, tech support) into base plans for at-risk segments to increase stickiness without aggressive discounting.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Help Win More Patents?
text:
Blueprinty is a small software company whose product helps engineering firms prepare and submit patent applications to the US Patent Office. Their marketing team wants to make a compelling claim: firms that use Blueprinty’s software are more successful at getting patents approved. That sounds like a reasonable hypothesis, but proving it is harder than it looks.
The ideal evidence would be a before-and-after comparison — measuring each firm’s patent success rate before they adopted the software and again after. That kind of panel data does not exist here. Instead, Blueprinty has collected cross-sectional data on 1,500 mature engineering firms, recording the number of patents each firm was awarded over the last five years, the firm’s geographic region, its age since incorporation, and whether or not it is currently a Blueprinty customer.
The catch is that Blueprinty’s customers are not selected at random. Firms that choose to buy the software may differ from those that do not in all sorts of ways — they may be older, more established, better resourced, or simply more active in patent filing. If customers tend to get more patents regardless of the software, then a raw comparison of patent counts between customers and non-customers would be misleading. Any difference we observe could reflect who Blueprinty’s customers happen to be rather than what the software actually does.
This post walks through how to address that problem using Poisson regression estimated by maximum likelihood. By controlling for firm age and region, we can get a cleaner estimate of the relationship between customer status and patent counts. The analysis is honest about its limitations: this is an observational study, not a randomized experiment, so we cannot fully rule out unobserved confounders.

section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
Before diving into the full regression, it helps to build intuition with a simpler model — one where we estimate a single patent rate \(\lambda\) for all firms.

Why the Poisson Distribution?
Patent counts are non-negative integers. A firm cannot receive \(-2\) patents or \(3.7\) patents. The Normal distribution, which is continuous and can be negative, is a poor fit for this kind of outcome. The Poisson distribution is the natural starting point for count data: it assigns probabilities to the integers \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\) and has a single parameter \(\lambda > 0\) that equals both the mean and the variance.
For a single observation \(Y\), the Poisson probability mass function is
\[
f(Y \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{Y}}{Y!}
\]


Likelihood and Log-Likelihood
Given \(n\) independent observations \(Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n\), the joint likelihood is the product of their individual probabilities:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\lambda \mid Y) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!} = e^{-n\lambda} \lambda^{\sum Y_i} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{Y_i!}
\]
Taking the natural log converts the product into a sum, which is much easier to work with:
\[
\ell(\lambda \mid Y) = \log \mathcal{L}(\lambda \mid Y) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\right) \log \lambda - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log(Y_i!)
\]


Coding the Log-Likelihood


Show Code
from scipy.special import gammaln  # log of factorial via log-gamma

def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y):
    """Log-likelihood of Poisson(lambda) for observed counts Y."""
    n = len(Y)
    return -n * lam + np.sum(Y) * np.log(lam) - np.sum(gammaln(Y + 1))




Visualizing the Log-Likelihood









The curve has a single peak — the log-likelihood is concave — and the maximum occurs near \(\lambda \approx 3.7\). This is how we “read” the MLE off the plot: it is simply the value of \(\lambda\) that sits at the top of the curve. The function drops off sharply for small \(\lambda\) and flattens gradually for large \(\lambda\), which reflects how the data constrain the estimate.


Analytical Solution
Taking the derivative of \(\ell\) with respect to \(\lambda\) and setting it to zero:
\[
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{\sum Y_i}{\lambda} = 0
\implies \hat{\lambda}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i = \bar{Y}
\]
The MLE is simply the sample mean — a reassuring result because the mean of a Poisson distribution is \(\lambda\), so it makes intuitive sense to estimate the parameter with the sample average.


Numerical Confirmation


Show Code
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

result = minimize_scalar(
    lambda lam: -poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y),
    bounds=(0.01, 20),
    method="bounded"
)

lambda_mle = result.x
lambda_mean = Y.mean()

print(f"Numerical MLE:  λ̂ = {lambda_mle:.4f}")
print(f"Sample mean:    Ȳ = {lambda_mean:.4f}")


Numerical MLE:  λ̂ = 3.6847
Sample mean:    Ȳ = 3.6847


The numerical optimizer recovers the sample mean to four decimal places, exactly as the calculus predicts. This gives us confidence that the optimization machinery is working correctly before we move to the more complex regression case.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Help Win More Patents?
text:
Poisson Regression
A single \(\lambda\) for all firms ignores the fact that different firms have different characteristics. A 10-year-old firm in the Northeast operating in a patent-intensive sector is unlikely to have the same patent rate as a 40-year-old firm in the Midwest. Poisson regression lets each firm have its own rate:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)
\]
The exponential link function is the key piece. The linear predictor \(X_i'\beta\) can take any real value, but \(\lambda_i\) must be strictly positive. Taking the exponential of \(X_i'\beta\) guarantees positivity while remaining differentiable everywhere — a clean, natural choice.

Building the Covariate Matrix


Show Code
regions = pd.get_dummies(df["region"], drop_first=True)

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "intercept": 1.0,
    "age": df["age"],
    "age_sq": df["age"] ** 2,
    "iscustomer": df["iscustomer"].astype(float),
})
X = pd.concat([X, regions.astype(float)], axis=1)
X_mat = X.values
Y_vec = df["patents"].values

print("Covariate matrix shape:", X_mat.shape)
print("Columns:", list(X.columns))

Columns: ['intercept', 'age', 'age_sq', 'iscustomer', 'Northeast', 'Northwest', 'South', 'Southwest']


A few design choices worth explaining:

Age squared is included because the relationship between firm age and patent activity is unlikely to be linear. Young firms ramp up over time; very old firms may plateau or slow down. The quadratic term captures this curvature.
One region is dropped (whichever get_dummies removes first) to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept. If we included dummies for all five regions plus an intercept, the five dummies would sum to a column of ones, making the design matrix rank-deficient.



Log-Likelihood for Poisson Regression


Show Code
def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    """Log-likelihood for Poisson regression with log link."""
    eta = X @ beta                    # linear predictor
    lam = np.exp(eta)                 # must be positive
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * eta - gammaln(Y + 1))




Finding the MLE with scipy.optimize


Show Code
beta_init = np.zeros(X_mat.shape[1])

result_reg = optimize.minimize(
    fun=lambda b: -poisson_regression_loglikelihood(b, Y_vec, X_mat),
    x0=beta_init,
    method="BFGS",
    options={"maxiter": 1000},
)

beta_hat = result_reg.x

hessian_approx = result_reg.hess_inv
se_hat = np.sqrt(np.diag(hessian_approx))


Standard errors come from the curvature of the log-likelihood at the maximum. Specifically, the observed information matrix is the negative of the Hessian of the log-likelihood, and the variance of the MLE is asymptotically equal to its inverse. Taking the square roots of the diagonal gives us coefficient-level standard errors.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Help Win More Patents?
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software
Regression coefficients in a Poisson model are not directly interpretable as “additional patents.” Because the model is multiplicative, the effect of customer status on expected patent count depends on all the other covariates through the exponential function. The right way to summarize the effect is through average marginal effects computed via counterfactual prediction.


Show Code
X0 = X_mat.copy()
X1 = X_mat.copy()

customer_col = list(X.columns).index("iscustomer")
X0[:, customer_col] = 0
X1[:, customer_col] = 1

y_hat_0 = np.exp(X0 @ glm_model.params)
y_hat_1 = np.exp(X1 @ glm_model.params)

avg_effect = (y_hat_1 - y_hat_0).mean()
print(f"Average predicted patents (non-customer):  {y_hat_0.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Average predicted patents (customer):      {y_hat_1.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Average treatment effect (ATE):            {avg_effect:.3f}")


Average predicted patents (non-customer):  3.436
Average predicted patents (customer):      4.229
Average treatment effect (ATE):            0.793











The procedure works as follows. We take every firm in the dataset and make two predictions: how many patents they would be expected to receive if they were not a customer, and how many they would be expected to receive if they were a customer — keeping age and region fixed at the firm’s actual values. The difference is the model’s estimate of how much the software matters for that particular firm. Averaging those firm-level differences over the whole sample gives us the average treatment effect.
The result: using Blueprinty’s software is associated with approximately {avg_effect:.2f} additional patents over a five-year period, after controlling for firm age and region.

A Careful Interpretation
This finding is consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim, but a few important caveats apply.
First, this is an observational study, not a randomized experiment. Even after controlling for age and region, there may be unobserved characteristics that differ between customers and non-customers — things like R&D budget, internal patent counsel, or the sector a firm operates in. If these unobserved factors are positively correlated with both software adoption and patent success, our estimate of the software’s effect would be overstated.
Second, the direction of causality is not guaranteed. It is possible that firms already inclined toward heavy patenting are also more likely to adopt patent-support software. In that case, the estimated coefficient would partly capture selection, not a causal effect of the software itself.
What the analysis does establish is that the association between Blueprinty customer status and patent counts is robust to controlling for age and region, and the estimated effect is economically meaningful. To make a stronger causal claim, one would ideally need either a randomized trial (offer the software to randomly selected firms) or a natural experiment — for instance, a price change that induced some firms to adopt the software for reasons unrelated to their underlying patent activity.
For now, the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive. Blueprinty’s software may well help engineering firms secure more patents; the data are consistent with that story. A well-designed randomized study would be the right next step to move from “consistent with” to “caused by.”

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MaxDiff, also called Best-Worst Scaling, is a survey method for measuring relative preferences. Instead of asking people to rate every option on a 1-10 scale, a MaxDiff task shows a small set of options and asks the respondent to choose the most preferred and least preferred item. In this survey, each screen showed 4 MSBA core classes, and students selected the class they liked most and least from that set.
This format is useful because people are often better at making trade-offs than at calibrating numeric ratings. A “7 out of 10” may mean different things to different people, but choosing the best and worst class from the same screen forces clearer differentiation.
In this post, I estimate student preferences for the 10 MSBA classes using three approaches:

A simple counts score: percent picked best minus percent picked worst.
A multinomial logit model estimated by maximum likelihood.
The same multinomial logit model estimated with a Bayesian Metropolis-Hastings sampler.

I expect the three methods to agree on the broad ranking, especially at the top and bottom. The bigger differences should appear in the middle, where several classes have similar preference strength.

section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
The counts analysis is intuitive, but it does not explicitly model the choice process. The multinomial logit model does. In an MNL model, each class receives a utility coefficient \(\beta_j\). When a respondent sees a set of classes, the probability that class \(j\) is picked as best is:
\[
P(j \text{ is best}) =
\frac{\exp(\beta_j)}
{\sum_{k \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_k)}.
\]
The worst choice can be treated as a second choice model with the utilities flipped. After removing the item chosen as best, the probability that item \(j\) is picked as worst is:
\[
P(j \text{ is worst} \mid \text{best}) =
\frac{\exp(-\beta_j)}
{\sum_{k \in \text{shown, } k \neq \text{best}} \exp(-\beta_k)}.
\]
The model is identified only up to a constant: adding the same number to every \(\beta\) leaves the choice probabilities unchanged. I therefore set item 1 as the reference class with \(\beta_1 = 0\) and estimate the other 9 coefficients.


Show code
task_groups = list(complete.groupby(["record_id", "task"], sort=False))

shown = np.vstack([
    group.sort_values("position")["item"].to_numpy(dtype=int) - 1
    for _, group in task_groups
])

best = np.array([
    int(group.loc[group["response"] == 1, "item"].iloc[0]) - 1
    for _, group in task_groups
])

worst = np.array([
    int(group.loc[group["response"] == -1, "item"].iloc[0]) - 1
    for _, group in task_groups
])

not_best_mask = shown != best[:, None]

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Maximum Likelihood
For each task, the log-likelihood is the log probability of the observed best choice plus the log probability of the observed worst choice:
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) =
\sum_{\text{tasks}}
\left[
\beta_{j_b^*}
- \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_j)
- \beta_{j_w^*}
- \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus j_b^*} \exp(-\beta_j)
\right].
\]
I maximize this likelihood with scipy.optimize.minimize, which is the Python equivalent of using optim() in R.


Show code
def full_beta(beta_free):
    return np.r_[0, beta_free]


def logsumexp_rows(values):
    row_max = np.max(values, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return (row_max + np.log(np.exp(values - row_max).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))).ravel()


def ll(beta_free):
    beta = full_beta(beta_free)

    best_part = beta[best] - logsumexp_rows(beta[shown])

    negative_utilities = -beta[shown]
    remaining_after_best = negative_utilities[not_best_mask].reshape(len(shown), 3)
    worst_part = -beta[worst] - logsumexp_rows(remaining_after_best)

    return (best_part + worst_part).sum()

text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation
For the Bayesian version, I use the same likelihood but add a weakly informative normal prior:
\[
\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim N(\boldsymbol{0}, 10I).
\]
The posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior:
\[
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid y) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta})\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}).
\]
I sample from this posterior with a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. I start the chain at the MLE because it is a high-likelihood region, then use a normal proposal step. I tuned the step size to 0.08, which gives an acceptance rate in the target range of about 25-40%.


Show code
def log_prior(beta_free):
    return np.sum(-0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * 10) - (beta_free ** 2) / (2 * 10))


def log_post(beta_free):
    return ll(beta_free) + log_prior(beta_free)


def metropolis(beta0, n_iter=15000, step=0.08, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    draws = np.empty((n_iter, len(beta0)))
    beta = beta0.copy()
    lp = log_post(beta)
    accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        proposal = beta + rng.normal(0, step, len(beta))
        proposal_lp = log_post(proposal)

        if np.log(rng.random()) < proposal_lp - lp:
            beta = proposal
            lp = proposal_lp
            accept += 1

        draws[t] = beta

    return draws, accept / n_iter

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Discussion
Substantively, the main finding is that students in this survey most preferred Marketing Analytics. Business Analytics and Customer Analytics also performed well, which suggests that applied analytics classes with clear business relevance are especially attractive to this group. At the lower end, Analytics Consulting and Marketing/Finance/Operations were selected as worst more often than best in the complete tasks.
Methodologically, each approach has a different use case. Counts are fast, transparent, and easy to explain in a dashboard. MLE MNL is better when I want a formal model, point estimates, and standard errors. Bayesian MNL is most helpful when I want uncertainty intervals for transformed quantities, or if I later want to extend the model to estimate individual-level preferences.
There are also caveats. The data come from a self-selected sample of MSBA students, so the results should not be generalized to every student. Preferences may depend on prior coursework, career goals, instructor familiarity, and where students are in the program. If I had more time, I would explore respondent-level heterogeneity: for example, whether students with more technical backgrounds rank programming-heavy classes differently from students with more business-oriented backgrounds.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Suppose you run a website with a landing page that invites visitors to subscribe to your newsletter. One small design choice on that page is the call to action (CTA): the short line of text that asks users to sign up. Even small changes in wording can affect behavior, so it is natural to ask which version of the CTA leads to more newsletter subscriptions.
In this post, I compare two possible CTAs. CTA A reads, “Sign up for our newsletter here!” and CTA B reads, “Stay up to date by signing up!” To evaluate which message performs better, I use an A/B test. In an A/B test, visitors are randomly assigned to one of two versions of a page or feature, and the outcomes in the two groups are compared. Here, the outcome is whether a visitor signs up for the newsletter. This simple setup provides a useful way to introduce several core ideas from classical frequentist statistics, including estimation, the Law of Large Numbers, the bootstrap, the Central Limit Theorem, and hypothesis testing.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
To study this A/B test statistically, I model each visitor’s outcome as a Bernoulli random variable. For any individual visitor, there are only two possible outcomes: either they sign up for the newsletter or they do not. If I code a sign-up as 1 and a non-sign-up as 0, then each observation can be thought of as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\pi\), where \(\pi\) is the probability of signing up.
Because the CTA may influence user behavior, I allow the sign-up probability to differ across the two groups. Let \(\pi_A\) denote the probability that a visitor signs up after seeing CTA A, and let \(\pi_B\) denote the probability of signing up after seeing CTA B. The main quantity of interest is the difference between these two probabilities,
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B.
\]
If \(\theta > 0\), CTA A performs better on average. If \(\theta < 0\), CTA B performs better. If \(\theta = 0\), then the two CTAs perform equally well.
In practice, the true probabilities \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\) are unknown, so we estimate them using sample averages. Since each observation is either 0 or 1, the sample mean is simply the sample proportion of sign-ups. That means our estimator for the treatment effect is
\[
\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B,
\]
where \(\bar{X}_A = \hat{\pi}_A\) is the observed sign-up rate in group A and \(\bar{X}_B = \hat{\pi}_B\) is the observed sign-up rate in group B. This difference in sample means will be the central object throughout the rest of the analysis.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real A/B test, we would not know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\). We would only observe a sample of user outcomes and try to learn about the underlying sign-up probabilities from that sample. For this exercise, however, it is helpful to set the true probabilities ourselves so that we can evaluate how well our statistical tools recover the truth.
Suppose the true sign-up probability is \(\pi_A = 0.22\) for CTA A and \(\pi_B = 0.18\) for CTA B. Then the true difference is
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B = 0.04.
\]
I now simulate 1,000 visitors in each group. Each simulated visitor either signs up (1) or does not sign up (0), according to the Bernoulli distribution for that group.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers says that as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean. In this setting, that idea matters because our estimator is built from sample means: \(\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\). If the sample size is large enough, we should expect this estimator to get closer to the true difference in sign-up probabilities.
To visualize this, I compute the element-wise difference between the simulated outcomes in group A and group B, producing a sequence of 1,000 differences. I then calculate the cumulative average of that sequence. This running mean shows how the estimate evolves as more and more observations are included.


Show code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

diff = A - B
running_mean = np.cumsum(diff) / np.arange(1, n + 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, n + 1), running_mean, linewidth=2)
plt.axhline(theta_true, linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Number of observations")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative average of A - B")
plt.title("Law of Large Numbers: Running Estimate of the CTA Effect")
plt.show()









At the beginning of the plot, the running average moves around quite a bit. That is exactly what we should expect: with only a small number of observations, random variation has a large influence on the estimate. As the sample size increases, however, the cumulative average becomes more stable and moves closer to the true value of 0.04.
The main takeaway is that noisy early results do not necessarily mean the estimator is unreliable. Instead, they reflect the fact that small samples are inherently variable. As more observations accumulate, random fluctuations begin to average out, and the estimate settles down. This is the practical value of the Law of Large Numbers in A/B testing: large samples make our estimates more trustworthy.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Once I have a point estimate of the treatment effect, the next question is how precise that estimate is. A single number such as \(\hat{\theta}\) tells me the estimated difference in sign-up rates, but it does not tell me how much uncertainty surrounds that estimate. To quantify that uncertainty, I need a standard error and, ideally, a confidence interval.
One useful way to estimate uncertainty is the bootstrap. The bootstrap is a resampling method that approximates the sampling variability of a statistic using the observed data itself. The basic idea is simple: repeatedly sample with replacement from the original data, recompute the statistic of interest for each resample, and then look at how much those resampled estimates vary. If the bootstrap estimates vary a lot, then the original estimator is not very precise; if they vary only a little, then the estimator is more stable.
Here, I repeatedly resample 1,000 observations from group A and 1,000 observations from group B, each time with replacement. For each bootstrap sample, I compute the difference in sample means, \(\hat{\theta}^* = \bar{X}_A^* - \bar{X}_B^*\). After repeating this process 1,000 times, I use the standard deviation of the 1,000 bootstrapped estimates as the bootstrapped standard error.


Show code
boot_thetas = []

for _ in range(1000):
    A_star = np.random.choice(A, size=n, replace=True)
    B_star = np.random.choice(B, size=n, replace=True)
    boot_thetas.append(A_star.mean() - B_star.mean())

boot_thetas = np.array(boot_thetas)

bootstrap_se = boot_thetas.std(ddof=1)

pA_hat = A.mean()
pB_hat = B.mean()

analytical_se = np.sqrt(
    pA_hat * (1 - pA_hat) / n +
    pB_hat * (1 - pB_hat) / n
)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * bootstrap_se
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * bootstrap_se

bootstrap_summary = pd.DataFrame({

        "Bootstrap standard error",

In this setting, the analytical standard error is available because the data are Bernoulli, but the bootstrap is especially useful more generally when a closed-form expression is difficult or unavailable.
Using the bootstrapped standard error, I construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\theta\) as \(\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times SE_{boot}\). This interval gives a range of plausible values for the true difference in sign-up rates. If the interval excludes 0, that suggests the data are consistent with a real difference between the two CTAs. If it includes 0, then the observed difference may simply reflect sampling variation.
The main idea is that point estimates alone are not enough. In A/B testing, it is just as important to report how uncertain the estimate is as it is to report the estimate itself.

text:
The Central Limit Theorem
:## The Central Limit Theorem
The Law of Large Numbers tells us that our estimator converges toward the truth as the sample size grows. The Central Limit Theorem adds another important piece: it tells us what the distribution of the estimator looks like across repeated samples. Even when the underlying data are not Normally distributed, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately Normal when the sample size is large enough. Since my estimator is the difference between two sample means, the same idea applies here as well.
This matters because much of classical frequentist inference relies on approximate Normality. If the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately bell-shaped, then I can use that fact to build confidence intervals and perform hypothesis tests.


Show code
sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
sim_results = {}

for sample_n in sample_sizes:
    theta_hats = []
    for _ in range(1000):
        A_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, sample_n)
        B_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, sample_n)
        theta_hats.append(A_sim.mean() - B_sim.mean())
    sim_results[sample_n] = np.array(theta_hats)

These four histograms show the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\theta}\) under repeated sampling for different sample sizes. When the sample size is small, the histogram can look rough, irregular, and somewhat asymmetric. That is not surprising: with only a small number of Bernoulli draws, the estimator can take on only a limited set of values, and randomness has a stronger visible effect.
As the sample size increases, the distribution becomes smoother, more concentrated, and more bell-shaped. By the time the sample size reaches 500, the distribution looks much closer to a Normal distribution. This is the Central Limit Theorem in action.
The practical takeaway is that large-sample inference becomes much more reliable because the distribution of the estimator is approximately Normal. That is exactly what will justify the z-based hypothesis test in the next section.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
The Central Limit Theorem gives us a practical way to move from estimation to formal inference. Once we know that the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately Normal in large samples, we can ask whether the observed difference between the two CTAs is large enough to count as evidence against the idea that the CTAs perform the same.
To formalize that question, I set up the null hypothesis
\[
H_0: \theta = 0,
\]
which says that the two CTAs have the same true sign-up rate. The alternative hypothesis is
\[
H_1: \theta \neq 0,
\]
which says that the two CTAs differ. A hypothesis test asks whether the observed data would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true.
To answer that question, I standardize the estimated treatment effect using its standard error:
\[
z = \frac{\hat{\theta} - 0}{SE(\hat{\theta})}.
\]
This standardization step has a clear logic. First, by the Central Limit Theorem, \(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately Normally distributed when the sample size is large. Second, under the null hypothesis, that distribution is centered at 0. Third, dividing by the standard error rescales the statistic into units of standard deviations, so under the null the resulting test statistic is approximately standard Normal, \(N(0,1)\). Once I know the null distribution of the test statistic, I can compute a p-value.
This procedure is sometimes loosely called a t-test, but in this setting it is more accurate to think of it as a large-sample z-test. The classical t-test comes from a setting where the data are Normally distributed and the variance is estimated from the sample, leading to an exact t-distribution. Here the data are Bernoulli, not Normal, so there is no exact t-distribution result. Instead, the Central Limit Theorem gives an approximate Normal reference distribution. In large samples the t-distribution and the standard Normal are extremely similar, so the practical difference is small, but the distinction is conceptually important.

A positive value means that CTA A outperformed CTA B in the simulated sample, while a negative value would mean the opposite. The p-value measures how surprising an estimate this large would be if the null hypothesis of no true difference were correct.
If the p-value is small, that means the observed difference would be unlikely under \(H_0\), giving evidence against the null. If the p-value is not small, then the data do not provide strong enough evidence to rule out the possibility that the observed difference is just random sampling variation. title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
It turns out that the two-sample comparison above can also be written as a simple linear regression. This is more than a mathematical curiosity. It shows that the same general regression machinery used throughout applied statistics can also be used to analyze A/B tests, and it explains why regression becomes such a flexible framework for experimental data.
To set this up, I stack the two groups into a single dataset. For each visitor, I define an outcome variable \(Y_i\) that equals 1 if the visitor signed up and 0 otherwise. I also define an indicator variable \(D_i\) that equals 1 if the visitor saw CTA A and 0 if the visitor saw CTA B. I then fit the regression
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i.
\]
The interpretation of the coefficients is straightforward. When \(D_i = 0\), the regression becomes \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \varepsilon_i\), so \(\beta_0\) is the mean outcome in group B and therefore estimates \(\pi_B\). When \(D_i = 1\), the expected outcome is \(\beta_0 + \beta_1\), which is the mean outcome in group A and therefore estimates \(\pi_A\). That means \(\beta_1\) must equal the difference in group means, \(\pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\). As a result, the OLS estimate \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is numerically identical to the difference-in-means estimator \(\hat{\theta}\).

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
In practice, one of the biggest temptations in A/B testing is to check the results before the experiment is finished. Suppose an impatient manager wants to look at the data after every 100 visitors in each group and stop the test as soon as the result becomes statistically significant at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level. At first glance, this may seem harmless. After all, each individual test is using the same 5% significance threshold.
The problem is that classical frequentist guarantees are built around a pre-specified testing procedure. A single hypothesis test conducted once at the end of the experiment has a 5% Type I error rate under the null. But if I repeatedly test the data as they accumulate, each additional peek creates another opportunity to get a false positive. The overall probability of rejecting the null at least once becomes much larger than 5%.
To see this clearly, I simulate a world in which the null hypothesis is actually true. I set \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\), so there is no real difference between the two CTAs. Then, within each simulated experiment, I check the p-value after 100, 200, 300, and so on up to 1,000 observations per group. If any one of those ten hypothesis tests is significant at the 5% level, I count that experiment as producing a false positive.


Show code
np.random.seed(42)

n_total = 1000
peek_points = np.arange(100, n_total + 1, 100)
n_experiments = 10000
pi_null = 0.20

false_positive_count = 0

for _ in range(n_experiments):
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)

    significant_any = False

    for k in peek_points:
        A_k = A_null[:k]
        B_k = B_null[:k]

        theta_k = A_k.mean() - B_k.mean()
        pA_k = A_k.mean()
        pB_k = B_k.mean()

        se_k = np.sqrt(
            pA_k * (1 - pA_k) / k +
            pB_k * (1 - pB_k) / k
        )

        if se_k == 0:
            continue

        z_k = theta_k / se_k
        p_k = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_k)))

        if p_k < 0.05:
            significant_any = True
            break

    if significant_any:
        false_positive_count += 1

peeking_false_positive_rate = false_positive_count / n_experiments

peeking_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "Nominal Type I error rate (single test)",
        "Empirical false positive rate with peeking"
    ],
    "Value": [
        0.05,
        peeking_false_positive_rate
    ]
})

Even though each individual test uses \(\alpha = 0.05\), the repeated testing strategy changes the overall procedure. Looking at the data multiple times without adjustment means that I am no longer running “a 5% test” in the usual sense.
This is the key lesson: statistical significance is not guaranteed to mean the same thing when the stopping rule is allowed to depend on the observed results. A result that appears significant after repeated peeking may simply be the product of chance rather than evidence of a real treatment effect.
In practice, this means that A/B tests should ideally use a pre-committed sample size and analysis plan, or else use methods specifically designed for sequential monitoring. Without those safeguards, repeated peeking can make experiments look more decisive than they really are.

title: Replication of Karlan and List (2007)
text:
Karlan and List (2007) conducted a large-scale natural field experiment to study whether the “price” of charitable giving—manipulated through matching grants—affects donor behavior. In partnership with a liberal US nonprofit organization, they sent direct mail solicitations to over 50,000 prior donors. Recipients were randomly assigned to either a control group (no match) or one of several treatment groups that varied by match ratio ($1:$1, $2:$1, or $3:$1), maximum matching grant amount ($25,000, $50,000, $100,000, or unstated), and suggested donation amount.
The key findings were:

Offering a match significantly increased both the response rate (by about 22%) and revenue per solicitation (by about 19%) relative to the control group.
Surprisingly, larger match ratios ($2:$1 and $3:$1) did not generate additional donations beyond the $1:$1 match—contradicting conventional fundraising wisdom.
The match effect was concentrated among donors in “red” (Republican-leaning) states, while donors in “blue” states showed little responsiveness to the match.

These results have important implications for fundraising strategy and for understanding the economics of charitable giving more broadly.

title: Replication of Karlan and List (2007)
text:
Conclusion
This replication confirms the three main findings of Karlan and List (2007):

Matching grants work: Simply announcing a match increases both response rates and revenue per solicitation.
Bigger matches don’t help more: There is no additional benefit to offering 2:1 or 3:1 matches over a 1:1 match, challenging the conventional wisdom among fundraisers.
Context matters: The treatment effect is driven by donors in red states, suggesting that social and political environment influences responsiveness to fundraising appeals.

These findings have practical implications: nonprofits can save money by using 1:1 matches instead of more generous ratios, and they should consider the political and social context of their donor base when designing campaigns.

Exploratory Data Analysis

Data Preprocessing
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler

# Scale Amount and Time (V1–V28 are already standardized)
rob_scaler = RobustScaler()
df["scaled_amount"] = rob_scaler.fit_transform(df[["Amount"]])
df["scaled_time"]   = rob_scaler.fit_transform(df[["Time"]])
df = df.drop(["Amount", "Time"], axis=1)

X, y = df.drop("Class", axis=1), df["Class"]

# Stratified 80/20 split
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

# Random undersampling → 50/50 fraud/non-fraud in training set only
rus = RandomUnderSampler(random_state=42)
X_train_res, y_train_res = rus.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)
Why undersample? Without rebalancing, a model trained on 99.83% non-fraud data simply learns to always predict “not fraud.” By reducing non-fraud training examples to match fraud count (492 each), we force the model to learn what distinguishes fraud. The test set stays imbalanced to reflect real deployment conditions.

Recall = 91.8% — catches 90 of 98 fraudulent transactions. The low precision (6%) is a direct consequence of the imbalance: even a small false-positive rate translates to thousands of mis-flagged legitimate transactions.

The PR curve is more informative than ROC for imbalanced data because it focuses on the minority class. The steep drop-off shows the bank’s fundamental tradeoff: higher recall = more false alarms.

title: Credit Card Fraud Detection
text:
Key Takeaways

Accuracy is misleading for imbalanced data. Always evaluate with Recall, Precision, and AUC.
Random undersampling works. Training on a balanced 50/50 subset forces models to learn fraud patterns rather than predicting the majority class.
High recall at the cost of precision is often the right call. Whether it’s worth flagging 1,402 legitimate transactions to catch 90 frauds depends on the bank’s cost structure — not the model’s accuracy.
Logistic Regression is a strong baseline. Before reaching for complex ensembles, a well-preprocessed Logistic Regression often performs surprisingly well.

title: Should Every Store Charge the Same Price?
text:
The question
Walk into two branches of the same supermarket chain and you will usually find the same price on the same can of soda. Dominick’s Finer Foods, a chain of about 90 stores in the Chicago area during the 1990s, priced this way most of the time. In half of all product-weeks in its soft-drink data, every store charged exactly the same price.
Its stores did not serve the same shoppers, though. Some sat in college towns along the North Shore, others in working-class suburbs to the west. If shoppers in some stores react less to price than shoppers in others, one price everywhere leaves money on the table.
This article asks two questions:

Should Dominick’s charge different prices in different stores?
If so, along what dimension should prices differ?

The analysis covers one product category, soft drinks: one segment of what a supermarket sells. Every elasticity, price and profit figure below is a soft-drink figure.






NoteKey results




Stores really differ in price sensitivity. Store elasticities run from −2.30 to −3.38, and most of that spread is real, not estimation noise.
Education is the clearest driver. Stores in more college-educated areas are less price-sensitive. Income has no effect of its own once education is held fixed.
Store-level prices raise soft-drink gross profit by 0.24%, about $1,100 a week across 86 stores, compared with the best single price.
Measured elasticity is the right dimension. Four store groups built on elasticity capture 76% of that gain. Dominick’s official price tiers capture 10%.
Every one of the 1,608 soft-drink products gets a price in every store. Within a store, all products move by the same percentage, from −3.7% to +4.0% under four groups.

section: Step 1: An elasticity for every store
text:
Step 1: An elasticity for every store

What an elasticity is
A price elasticity measures how strongly unit sales react to price, in percentage terms:
\[
\text{elasticity} = \frac{\%\ \text{change in units sold}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}
\]
Take the best-selling item in the data, a 24-pack of Pepsi cans at about $6.09. Suppose a store’s elasticity is −2.8 and it sells 100 packs a week. Raising the price by 1%, to $6.15, cuts sales by about 2.8%, to roughly 97 packs. Revenue falls too, by about 1% − 2.8% = −1.8%, because the volume loss is larger than the price gain. Any elasticity below −1 is called elastic: price increases lose revenue. The closer the elasticity is to zero, the less shoppers react to price.


Why the model is written in logs
Percentages are awkward to put into a regression, but logarithms turn them into plain differences: a small change in \(\log x\) is approximately the percentage change in \(x\). So if demand follows
\[
q = A \cdot p^{\beta} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \log q = \log A + \beta \log p,
\]
the slope \(\beta\) of \(\log q\) on \(\log p\) is exactly the elasticity. This form also assumes the elasticity is the same at every price, which is called constant elasticity. A comparison of functional forms supports it here: a semi-log model, where only sales are logged, fits clearly worse, and adding a squared log-price term barely improves the fit (within-R² of 0.301 vs. 0.298).


The model, store by store
For each store \(s\), I regress weekly log units on log price for every soft-drink product the store sells:
\[
\log q_{ut} = \alpha_u + \delta_t + \beta_s \log p_{ut} + \varepsilon_{ut}
\qquad \text{(estimated separately for each store } s\text{)}
\]








Symbol
Meaning
Example




\(u\), \(t\)
Product (UPC) and week
Pepsi 24-pack cans; week 250


\(q_{ut}\)
Units of product \(u\) sold in week \(t\) (MOVE)
120 packs


\(p_{ut}\)
Unit price of product \(u\) in week \(t\) (PRICE / QTY)
$5.99 per pack


\(\alpha_u\)
Product fixed effect: a separate intercept for each product, its normal sales level in this store
Pepsi 24-packs always sell far more than a niche ginger ale


\(\delta_t\)
Week fixed effect: a separate intercept for each week, capturing anything that moves all soft-drink sales in this store that week
A hot July 4th week lifts every product


\(\beta_s\)
Store \(s\)’s price elasticity, the quantity of interest
−2.8


\(\varepsilon_{ut}\)
Everything the model does not explain
A local event, a stock-out



What the fixed effects buy. Without them, the regression would compare different products: cheap 2-liter bottles sell many units and expensive 24-packs fewer, which would look like price sensitivity even if no shopper ever reacted to a price change. With a product effect, each product is compared only with itself. With a week effect, a week when everything sells more (a holiday, a heat wave) is not mistaken for a price response. What remains is the question the elasticity should answer: in weeks when this product was cheaper than usual in this store, compared with how that week went for the store’s other soft drinks, did it sell more than usual, and by how much? \(\beta_s\) averages that response across all products in the store.
What “store elasticity” means. \(\beta_s\) is the typical own-price elasticity of a soft-drink product in store \(s\). It includes shoppers who switch to another soft drink in the same store when one product gets more expensive, which is why it is larger in size than an elasticity for soft drinks as a whole would be.
How much data each store has. A typical store contributes about 128,000 product-weeks (between 50,000 and 154,000), covering about 1,200 products over roughly 380 weeks.
Standard errors are clustered by product within each store. The same product observed in many weeks is not treated as many independent pieces of evidence.

  const curve = s => xs.map(x => ({store: s.store, city: s.city, x, y: 100 * Math.pow(1 + x / 100, s.elasticity)}))
  const all = pricingStores.flatMap(curve)
  const at = s => 100 * Math.pow(1 + priceMove / 100, s.elasticity) - 100
  return html`<div>
  <p style="margin:0 0 .5rem 0">A <b>${pct(priceMove, 0)}</b> price change moves unit sales by
  <b style="color:#0d366b">${pct(at(most))}</b> in store ${most.store} (${most.city}) and by
  <b style="color:#2a78d6">${pct(at(least))}</b> in store ${least.store} (${least.city}).</p>
  ${P.plot({
    width, height: 360, style: chartStyle, marginBottom: 50, marginRight: 120,
    x: {labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 40, label: "Price change (%)", domain: [-10, 10]},
    y: {label: "Unit sales index (today = 100)", grid: true},
    marks: [
      P.line(all, {x: "x", y: "y", z: "store", stroke: "#bbb", strokeWidth: 0.8, strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
      P.line(curve(most), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#0d366b", strokeWidth: 2}),
      P.line(curve(least), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2}),
      P.ruleX([priceMove], {stroke: "#eb6834", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      P.dot([most, least], {x: () => priceMove, y: s => 100 + at(s), fill: (s, i) => i ? "#2a78d6" : "#0d366b", r: 5, stroke: "white"}),
      P.text([most], {x: () => 10, y: s => 100 * Math.pow(1.1, s.elasticity), text: s => `Store ${s.store}, e = ${s.elasticity.toFixed(2)}`, textAnchor: "start", dx: 6, fill: "#0d366b"}),
      P.text([least], {x: () => 10, y: s => 100 * Math.pow(1.1, s.elasticity), text: s => `Store ${s.store}, e = ${s.elasticity.toFixed(2)}`, textAnchor: "start", dx: 6, fill: "#2a78d6"}),
      P.tip(all, P.pointer({x: "x", y: "y", channels: {Store: "store", City: "city"}, format: {x: d => `${d}%`, y: d => d.toFixed(1)}}))
    ]
  })}</div>`
}







Because the model assumes a constant elasticity, the outer parts of the chart are extrapolations. That is one reason the pricing step later limits price changes to ±10%.

title: Should Every Store Charge the Same Price?
text:
Are the differences real?
Every estimate comes with noise, so a spread across 86 stores could appear even if all stores were identical. Two checks address this.
A heterogeneity test compares the spread of the estimates with their standard errors:
\[
Q = \sum_s w_s \left(\hat\beta_s - \bar\beta\right)^2, \qquad w_s = \frac{1}{\mathrm{se}_s^2}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(\hat\beta_s\), \(\mathrm{se}_s\)
Store \(s\)’s estimated elasticity and its standard error


\(\bar\beta\)
Precision-weighted average elasticity


\(Q\)
Weighted spread; if all stores were truly identical, \(Q\) would be close to the number of stores minus one


\(\tau\)
Standard deviation of the true elasticities, after removing the part of the spread that noise explains



For the 86 stores, \(Q = 485\) against about 85 expected under no real differences (p < 10⁻⁵⁰). The true spread is \(\tau = 0.23\), against a typical standard error of 0.12. About 80% of the observed variance is real.
Robustness checks re-estimate every store under different choices and compare the rankings:








Alternative estimate

+0.42

0.97

The promotion check moves every store, so it is worth a closer look. Sales jump in promotion weeks partly because of the promotion itself (displays, ads), not only because of the lower price. The simple model credits that jump to the price cut. Adding a promotion dummy and a promotion × price term removes it, and every store becomes about 0.4 less elastic. The ranking of stores barely changes. In the chart, the dashed line is where both estimates would be equal.

      channels: {Store: "store", City: "city"}, tip: {format: {fill: false, x: d => d.toFixed(2), y: d => d.toFixed(2)}}})

section: Step 2: What makes a store more price-sensitive?
text:
Step 2: What makes a store more price-sensitive?
Knowing that stores differ is half the story. The second model asks which store characteristics go with higher or lower sensitivity. It pools all stores and lets the price coefficient depend on store characteristics:
\[
\log q_{ust} = a_{us} + d_t + b_0 \log p_{ust} + \sum_k \gamma_k \, Z_{ks} \log p_{ust} + \varepsilon_{ust}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(a_{us}\)
Fixed effect for each product in each store (about 105,000 of them)


\(d_t\)
Week fixed effect


\(Z_{ks}\)
Characteristic \(k\) of store \(s\), standardized across stores (mean 0, standard deviation 1)


\(b_0\)
Elasticity of a store with average characteristics


\(\gamma_k\)
Change in elasticity when characteristic \(k\) rises by one standard deviation



A store’s elasticity is therefore \(b_0 + \sum_k \gamma_k Z_{ks}\). A positive \(\gamma_k\) means less price-sensitive, because it moves the elasticity toward zero. The characteristics do not appear on their own because \(a_{us}\) already absorbs anything fixed about a store; they can only enter through their interaction with price. Standard errors are clustered by store, since the characteristics vary only across the 83 stores with demographic data.

The store characteristics
Each store’s trading area is described by 1990 census figures in the store file. The table gives each characteristic’s average and range across the 83 stores with demographic data, and what one standard deviation (SD), the unit behind every \(\gamma_k\), means in plain terms.

Alone vs. together
Each characteristic is tested twice:

Alone: the model contains only that one characteristic. Its coefficient picks up everything that travels with it. If educated areas also have higher incomes, the “alone” coefficient on education partly reflects income too.

Reading each characteristic
Education: the main driver. One SD more college graduates (11 percentage points) moves the elasticity by +0.12 with the other characteristics held fixed. The average store sits at about −2.77, so a store one SD above average in education is at about −2.65: a 1% price increase costs it about 2.65% of volume instead of 2.77%. Across the full range, from the least educated area (5% graduates) to the most educated (53%), that is a difference of about 0.5 in elasticity, more than twice the true spread across stores. The effect is significant alone and together, and in every variant of the model, including the ones that swap income for no-car share or poverty.
Why would educated areas be less price-sensitive? Comparing prices takes time, and the time of college-educated shoppers is worth more on the job market, so shopping around costs them more. Education may also capture long-run income and wealth better than one year’s median income. The store file’s shopper-type indices (hurried, avid and constrained shoppers) could test the time-cost explanation directly.
Income: no effect of its own. Alone, income’s coefficient is +0.011 with p = 0.60: richer areas are not measurably less price-sensitive. Together, it turns negative (−0.061, p = 0.03). The sign flip comes from the 0.66 correlation with education. Alone, income borrows some of education’s effect. Once education is held fixed, the remaining comparison is between two equally educated areas with different incomes, and there the richer one is slightly more price-sensitive. The practical reading: income by itself is not what makes a store less sensitive. Education is.
No-car share and poverty: income seen from the other side. Both are strongly negatively correlated with income (−0.83 and −0.90). When either replaces income in the joint model, it takes a positive coefficient (+0.072 and +0.061), the mirror image of income’s −0.061. The data cannot separate these three; they carry one shared signal about an area’s economic position.
Household size: possible, not confirmed. Alone, larger households go with higher price sensitivity (−0.071, p < 0.001), which fits the idea that families buying more soda feel price more. Together, the coefficient shrinks to −0.026 and is no longer significant (p = 0.26). Household size moves with car ownership (−0.55), age (−0.37) and income (0.32), and once those are held fixed too little of its own effect remains to be sure it is real.
Age 60+: no detectable effect. Neither alone (+0.007, p = 0.71) nor together (+0.033, p = 0.12). Retirees may have more time to compare prices but also differ in many other ways, and on balance no effect shows up.
Distance to Cub Foods: no detectable effect. If a nearby discount competitor made shoppers more price-sensitive, stores farther from Cub Foods would be less sensitive, a positive coefficient. The estimates are close to zero alone (+0.009, p = 0.67) and together (−0.016, p = 0.40). One possible reason is that Dominick’s already prices its CubFighter stores, those facing Cub Foods directly, about 3% lower, which may absorb part of the competitive pressure.


See it store by store
Pick a characteristic to plot against each store’s own elasticity from Step 1. The line is a simple linear fit.

  const r = d3.sum(data, d => (d[charPick] - mx) * (d.elasticity - my)) /
    Math.sqrt(d3.sum(data, d => (d[charPick] - mx) ** 2) * d3.sum(data, d => (d.elasticity - my) ** 2))
  const label = drivers.find(d => d.factor === charPick).label
  return html`<div><p style="margin:0 0 .5rem 0">Correlation with store elasticity across ${data.length} stores: <b>r = ${r.toFixed(2)}</b></p>
  ${P.plot({
    width, height: 360, style: chartStyle, marginBottom: 50,
    x: {label, grid: true}, y: {label: "Store elasticity", grid: true},
    marks: [
      P.linearRegressionY(data, {x: charPick, y: "elasticity", stroke: "#eb6834", fill: "#eb6834", fillOpacity: 0.1}),
      P.dot(data, {x: charPick, y: "elasticity", fill: "#2a78d6", r: 4, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 0.8,
        channels: {Store: "store", City: "city"}, tip: {format: {x: d => d.toFixed(3), y: d => d.toFixed(2)}}})
    ]
  })}</div>`
}







How much do characteristics explain? Regressing each store’s elasticity on the five characteristics, weighted by precision, gives an R² of 37% across 83 stores. The biggest misses are the most elastic stores. Six stores with short histories (fewer than 300 weeks) account for much of this: without them, R² rises to 54%. So demographics explain a good part of the differences, but far from all of them. That matters for pricing.

title: Should Every Store Charge the Same Price?
text:
Step 3: From elasticity to price
The pricing step follows a simple counterfactual. Start from one price per product, the same in every store. Then let each store, or each group of stores, move its prices and see how much gross profit changes.
Price index. Each product’s base price \(\bar p_u\) is its chain-average price (revenue / units across all stores and weeks). A store’s prices are written as a multiple \(r\) of the base price, so \(r = 1\) is the chain-average price and \(r = 1.05\) is 5% above it. All products in a store move by the same percentage. This keeps relative prices inside the store unchanged, so the model does not need to know how shoppers switch between products.
Profit of a store at price index \(r\), with a constant elasticity:
\[
\pi_s(r) = (r - k)\, R_s\, r^{\,e_s}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(r\)
Price index (1 = chain-average price)


\(k\)
Unit cost as a share of the chain-average price


\(R_s\)
Store \(s\)’s weekly soft-drink revenue at the chain-average price


\(e_s\)
Store \(s\)’s elasticity (shrunk; see below)


\((r - k)\)
Margin per dollar of base price


\(R_s r^{e_s}\)
Sales (in base-price dollars) after the price moves to \(r\)



The best price. Setting the derivative to zero, \(\frac{d\pi_s}{dr} = R_s r^{e_s - 1}\left[r + e_s(r - k)\right] = 0\), gives the textbook markup rule:
\[
r^*_s = \frac{k\,|e_s|}{|e_s| - 1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\frac{r^*_s - k}{r^*_s} = \frac{1}{|e_s|}
\]
The right-hand form is the Lerner condition: the best margin equals one over the elasticity. Less price-sensitive stores (smaller \(|e_s|\)) get higher prices. When a group of stores must share one price, the shared price maximizes the group’s total profit \(\sum_{s \in g} \pi_s(r)\). It is found numerically and sits between the members’ own best prices, weighted by revenue.
Try it below: drag the elasticity and watch where profit peaks. The two grey curves are the most and least price-sensitive stores. Notice how flat the curves are near the top.


Show code
viewof eTry = Inputs.range([-3.6, -2.2], {step: 0.01, value: -2.78, label: "Store elasticity"})









Show code
{
  const xs = d3.range(0.85, 1.1501, 0.0025)
  const rel = (r, e) => 100 * ((r - K) * Math.pow(r, e) / (1 - K) - 1)
  const best = e => Math.min(1.1, Math.max(0.9, K * Math.abs(e) / (Math.abs(e) - 1)))
  const ext = pricingStores.slice().sort((a, b) => a.elasticity_shrunk - b.elasticity_shrunk)
  const refs = [ext[0], ext[ext.length - 1]]
  const refLines = refs.flatMap(s => xs.map(r => ({store: s.store, x: 100 * (r - 1), y: rel(r, s.elasticity_shrunk)})))
  const line = xs.map(r => ({x: 100 * (r - 1), y: rel(r, eTry)}))
  const rb = best(eTry)
  return html`<div><p style="margin:0 0 .5rem 0">With elasticity <b>${eTry.toFixed(2)}</b> and cost at 64% of the base price,
  the best price is <b>${pct(100 * (rb - 1))}</b>, and it earns <b>${pct(rel(rb, eTry), 2)}</b> more profit than the chain-average price.</p>
  ${P.plot({
    width, height: 360, style: chartStyle, marginBottom: 50,
    x: {labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 40, label: "Price change from chain average (%)"},
    y: {label: "Profit change vs. chain-average price (%)", grid: true, domain: [-12, 4]},
    clip: true,
    marks: [
      P.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#999"}),
      P.line(refLines, {x: "x", y: "y", z: "store", stroke: "#bbb", strokeWidth: 1.2}),
      P.text(refs, {x: s => 100 * (best(s.elasticity_shrunk) - 1), y: s => rel(best(s.elasticity_shrunk), s.elasticity_shrunk), text: s => `Store ${s.store}`, dy: -10, fill: "#888"}),
      P.line(line, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      P.dot([rb], {x: r => 100 * (r - 1), y: r => rel(r, eTry), fill: "#eb6834", r: 6, stroke: "white"}),
      P.tip(line, P.pointer({x: "x", y: "y", format: {x: d => `${d.toFixed(1)}%`, y: d => `${d.toFixed(2)}%`}}))
    ]
  })}</div>`
}








Two safeguards
Before the markup rule turns elasticities into prices, two adjustments protect the result from the model’s own weaknesses: noise in the estimates, and a demand curve that is only reliable close to observed prices.

Safeguard 1: Shrink noisy elasticities toward the mean
The problem: the optimizer’s curse. Every store elasticity is an estimate with some error. When prices are set from estimates, the stores that look the most extreme are, on average, the ones whose errors happened to push them outward. The pricing rule then gives those stores the largest price changes, and it predicts gains that will not show up in reality, because part of the extremeness was noise. Decision scientists call this the optimizer’s curse (or the winner’s curse). It appears whenever the option that looks best is picked from noisy estimates, and it is a known issue in data-driven pricing, targeting and A/B testing.
The fix: empirical-Bayes shrinkage. The standard remedy is to pull each estimate toward the group average by an amount that depends on how noisy it is. A classic demonstration comes from baseball: early-season batting averages, shrunk toward the league average, predicted players’ rest-of-season averages better than the raw early-season numbers. The same logic applies to stores. A store whose estimate is precise keeps most of its own value; a store with a noisy estimate is pulled further toward the chain mean:
\[
e^{\text{shrunk}}_s = \mu + w_s\left(\hat\beta_s - \mu\right),
\qquad w_s = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \mathrm{se}_s^2}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(\hat\beta_s\)
Store \(s\)’s raw elasticity from Step 1


\(\mu\)
Chain mean elasticity, weighted by precision (about −2.79)


\(\tau\)
Spread of the true store elasticities, from the heterogeneity test (0.23)


\(\mathrm{se}_s\)
Store \(s\)’s standard error: how noisy its estimate is


\(w_s\)
Weight on the store’s own estimate, between 0 and 1



The weight has a direct reading. \(\tau^2\) is the real variation across stores and \(\mathrm{se}_s^2\) is the noise in store \(s\)’s estimate, so \(w_s\) is the share of the store’s observed distance from the mean that is believed to be real. Here the weights run from 0.59 for the noisiest store to 0.94 for the most precise, with a median of 0.80. The largest adjustment is store 59 (Crystal Lake), whose raw estimate of −3.12 has a standard error of 0.16 and moves to −3.01. The median store moves by only 0.02.
The chart shows each store’s raw estimate (grey) and shrunk estimate (blue), sorted by the raw value. Hover to see the numbers.


Show code
{
  const data = pricingStores.slice().sort((a, b) => a.elasticity - b.elasticity)
    .map(d => ({...d, w: 0.2294 ** 2 / (0.2294 ** 2 + d.se ** 2), id: String(d.store)}))
  return P.plot({
    width, height: Math.max(420, data.length * 6.2), marginLeft: 10, marginTop: 28, style: chartStyle, marginBottom: 50,
    x: {labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 40, label: "Elasticity  →  less price-sensitive", domain: [-3.45, -2.2], grid: true},
    y: {domain: data.map(d => d.id), axis: null},
    marks: [
      P.ruleX([-2.789], {stroke: "#eb6834", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
      P.text([-2.789], {x: d => d, frameAnchor: "top", dy: -4, dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", text: () => "chain mean μ", fill: "#eb6834"}),
      P.arrow(data, {y1: "id", y2: "id", x1: "elasticity", x2: "elasticity_shrunk", stroke: "#86b6ef", headLength: 4, strokeWidth: 1.2}),
      P.dot(data, {y: "id", x: "elasticity", fill: "#bbb", r: 3}),
      P.dot(data, {y: "id", x: "elasticity_shrunk", fill: "#2a78d6", r: 3.5, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 0.6,
        channels: {Store: "store", City: "city", Raw: d => d.elasticity.toFixed(2), "Std. error": d => d.se.toFixed(3), "Weight on own estimate": d => d.w.toFixed(2)},
        tip: {format: {y: false, x: d => d.toFixed(2)}}})
    ]
  })
}







Shrinkage narrows the spread of store elasticities from an SD of 0.20 to 0.17, so the recommended prices are a little less extreme. It also matters for the reported gain: with raw elasticities, store-level pricing would appear to earn 0.35% instead of 0.24%. Much of that difference is noise that would not turn into real profit, which is exactly what the optimizer’s curse predicts.


Safeguard 2: Cap price changes at ±10%
The problem: the demand curve is only trustworthy near observed prices. A constant-elasticity curve is a convenient approximation that fits well in the range of prices the stores actually charged. Taken far outside that range, it keeps applying the same percentage response at any price, which real demand rarely does. Research in marketing has shown that this matters for pricing: log-log demand models fit the data well, but an optimizer working with them tends to recommend prices outside the observed range, where the model has no evidence and its predictions are least reliable. Practical pricing systems handle this with guardrails, bounds on how far a recommended price may move from current prices.
The fix: keep prices where the data are. Store prices may move at most ±10% from the best single price. That bound is well inside what the data cover: half of all observed weekly prices lie within ±10% of that product’s average price in the same store, and the middle 90% span about −29% to +28%, mostly because of promotions. So every recommended price sits in a range the model has seen many times.
The cap binds for only two stores, 33 (Chicago) and 137 (Evanston). The markup rule would put them about 11% to 12% above the chain price, and the cap holds them at +10%. Removing the cap changes the total store-level gain by less than 0.003 percentage points. The cap is a guardrail, not a driver of the results.



Choosing the cost
Cost matters for the price level. With an elasticity around −2.8, the markup rule says the best margin is \(1/2.8 \approx 36\%\). Dominick’s actual regular-week margin is 17%. So if the data’s own cost is used, the model says every soft-drink price is too low. That level effect would swamp the question this article is about, which is whether prices should differ across stores.
The main case therefore calibrates the cost so that today’s chain-average price is already the best single price. Setting \(\frac{d}{dr}\sum_s \pi_s(r) = 0\) at \(r = 1\) and solving for \(k\):
\[
k = 1 + \frac{\sum_s R_s}{\sum_s R_s e_s} = 1 - \frac{1}{|\bar e_R|} = 0.640
\]
where \(\bar e_R\) is the revenue-weighted average elasticity. The table compares this with two alternatives:

from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

def profit(r, k, R, e):
    """Gross profit at price index r with unit cost k (share of base price)."""
    return (r - k) * R * r ** e

def calibrated_cost(R, e):
    """Cost share that makes the chain-average price the best single price."""
    return 1 + R.sum() / (R * e).sum()

def best_price(k, R, e, lo, hi):
    """Best shared price for a group of stores."""
    res = minimize_scalar(lambda r: -profit(r, k, R, e).sum(),
                          bounds=(lo, hi), method="bounded")
    return res.x

# Empirical-Bayes shrinkage
weight_own = tau**2 / (tau**2 + se**2)
e_shrunk = mu + weight_own * (e_raw - mu)

title: Should Every Store Charge the Same Price?
text:
What the analysis says
Should Dominick’s charge different prices in different stores? Store-level prices add 0.24% to soft-drink gross profit, about $1,100 a week across 86 stores. Four elasticity-based price groups deliver three quarters of that.
Along what dimension? By measured price sensitivity. The least sensitive stores get up to 10% higher prices, and the most sensitive about 8% lower. Official tiers, price zones and demographic groupings capture 10% to 30% of the possible gain.
What drives sensitivity? Education is the clearest driver: more college-educated areas are less price-sensitive. Income, car ownership and poverty carry one shared signal that education largely absorbs. Characteristics explain 37% to 54% of the store differences, which is why grouping stores by demographics captures less of the gain than grouping by measured elasticity.
Price level. With the data’s own costs, the best single price is 29% above today’s average, worth +31% in gross profit. That is more than 100 times the gain from store-level prices under the same cost.

Limits

The same estimates set and judge the prices. Shrinkage reduces the resulting optimism, but a true holdout test would estimate on earlier weeks and evaluate on later ones.
One category, product-level elasticities. The elasticities include shoppers switching between soft drinks in the same store. When all products move together, real volume losses are likely smaller, which matters most for the price-level result.
What is not modeled: effects on other categories, competitor reactions, and shoppers switching to a cheaper nearby Dominick’s. The last would shrink the store-level gain.
Assumed shapes. Constant elasticity is assumed, so results are only trusted within ±10% of today’s prices. Cost is a fixed share of price for every product.
Associations, not causes. Prices were not randomly assigned, so the drivers of elasticity are associations.
Gross profit only. Labor, rent and other operating costs are not included.
